extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in German media, journalism history, and magazine studies
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarising Stern (magazine): its history, journalistic style, editorial stance, major scandals, circulation trends, and format/production practices. Useful for understanding editorial standards and performance metrics of a German weekly news magazine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nutzwertiger Journalismus ('useful journalism')
rubrics_metrics.description: Stern sought to present itself as an exemplar of what in Germany is called nutzwertiger Journalismus ('useful journalism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis is on providing sufficient background on a topic to allow readers opportunity to arrive at their own judgements rather than have these decided for them editorially. This principle shapes topic selection and reporting style (longer, background-rich pieces rather than sensational headlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article length and investigative depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles tended to be longer and more investigative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer investigative pieces provide background and context for readers; this is contrasted with tabloid-style headlines. Such depth is part of the magazine's journalistic standard and identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of topics (social and life-style coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguished from Der Spiegel by the wider range of social and life-style issues covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial selection values a broader social/lifestyle remit alongside political/current-affairs reporting, affecting what counts as suitable content for the magazine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustration and graphic design
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater reliance on illustration and graphic design to distinguish the magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavier use of illustration, arresting large-print photography, sidebars and infographics is a deliberate stylistic criterion; visual presentation is a key part of Stern's editorial value and reader appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial safeguards and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hitler Diaries fiasco revealed management's bypassing of traditional editorial channels and safeguards; scientific examination proved the diaries were forgeries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong editorial verification procedures and adherence to established editorial channels are implicit requirements to maintain accuracy and credibility. The Hitler Diaries example is an anti-pattern: failure to authenticate costly/sensational acquisitions can lead to resignations, staff protest and long-term reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of 'sensation-seeking' or 'check book journalism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-scandal Stern became a byword for the folly and hazards of 'sensation-seeking check book journalism'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchasing sensational materials (rather than rigorously verifying them) is presented as a practice that undermines journalistic integrity and must be avoided; credibility is hard to regain after such practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocative cover imagery and political provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stern has used provocative covers (e.g., photo-shopped image of Donald Trump giving a Nazi salute with the headline 'Sein Kampf'), generating controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provocative covers can attract attention but also invite criticism (e.g., from Jewish leaders and the Simon Wiesenthal Center) for potentially diminishing or misappropriating historical atrocities. The magazine's defense frames such visuals as commentary on current political behaviour; editors must weigh provocation against ethical/historical sensitivities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial stance and willingness to question consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly left-liberal editorial stance and willingness to question the post-war political and social order (e.g., breaking silence on National-Socialist past, openness to student protest perspectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit editorial position (left-liberal, readiness to challenge established consensus) functions as a criterion for story selection and framing; readers and critics evaluate the magazine relative to this stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of press freedom and editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: During the 1962 Spiegel affair Stern (with others) offered Der Spiegel presses, teletypes and office space so it could continue publishing while being investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support for press freedom and practical solidarity with other outlets is presented as part of the magazine's journalistic ethics and professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of women and dignity in imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Stern's 'cover-girl' tradition was criticised (Alice Schwarzer's 1978 lawsuit) as denying the human dignity of women by presenting them 'as a mere sexual object'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial choices about photographic depiction of women are subject to ethical scrutiny; practices perceived as objectifying can provoke legal/ public backlash and should be reconsidered despite legal limits on prosecution. The episode led editors to 'think' about such practices—an implicit call for more respectful portrayal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation, e-paper and advertising metrics as measures of success
rubrics_metrics.description: The article reports print circulation figures (peak 1.5–1.8 million historically, falling to under half a million by 2019; detailed year-by-year figures) and advertising revenue declines (218 million euros in 2003 to 107.3 million euros by 2020). E-paper circulation grew from ~8,500 in 2015 Q2 to ~26,800 in Q4 2020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation numbers, e-paper subscriptions and advertising revenue are presented as primary quantitative metrics for evaluating the magazine's commercial health and reach. The text also notes that 'actual readership' exceeds copies sold, indicating that multiple metrics (sales + estimated readership) matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to online conventions and format reformatting
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2013 reformatting of the printed edition mimics online features and conventions: greater use of sidebars and infographics, less formal language, and greater emphasis on large-print photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapting print format and language to reflect online consumption patterns is an editorial and design criterion aimed at retaining readers; format choices (infographics, sidebars, tone) are evaluated by their effectiveness in engaging contemporary audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and reputation as central evaluative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Stern's credibility was 'seriously damaged' by the Hitler Diaries scandal and 'it took the magazine many years to regain its pre-scandal status and reputation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions are ultimately judged by their impact on credibility and reputation; restoring trust after major errors is difficult and is a central metric for long-term assessment of a news magazine.
